children: This screen grab made on September 9, 2026, from a handout video released by the U.S. Central Command on September 8, 2026, shows what the U.S. military says is a strike on an Iranian tanker in the Gulf of Oman.
Oil prices hit $100 a barrel on Wednesday after the war worsened between the U.S. and Iran amid a fresh round of strikes.

Brent crude's November contract (BRN00) (BRNX26) briefly touched $100.18 a barrel before retreating slightly below the threshold to $99.95. It brings the international benchmark to its highest level since July 23.
Meanwhile, West Texas Intermediate's October contract (CL.1) (CLV26) advanced by more than 1% to $94.26 a barrel, its most expensive since the beginning of June.
Both Brent crude and WTI are now up over 60% since the start of the year, and about 10% since just the start of September, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

The moves come after the U.S. Central Command announced late Tuesday that it attacked five Iranian crude oil vessels - four in the Gulf of Oman and one near Kharg Island, where 90% of the country's oil exports are handled - after it said Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps targeted a U.S. Navy warship two times in the last two days with ballistic missiles.

Tehran said it responded by launching strikes at a U.S. military base in Jordan, eight ships - including two U.S. Navy vessels - and eight oil tankers it claimed were attempting to pass through a "prohibited and unsafe" part of the Strait of Hormuz.

"Iran continues to try to hit U.S. naval ships," U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters in Colombia on Tuesday. "And, for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers. And I think you'll see that again today."

"With Brent now up more than 60% year-to-date, renewed security concerns around the Strait of Hormuz are tightening the market's focus on supply fragility, energy pass-through and the return of stagflation risk," Patrick Munnelly, market strategist at Tickmill Group, wrote in a note Wednesday.

It also followed Saudi Arabia's Saudi Aramco halting operations at some of its oil refineries in the country after Yemen's Houthi rebels attacked energy and civilian sites in Jazan, Najran, Abha and Khamis Mushait, wounding 73 people. The group accused Saudi Arabia of attacking a prison in the northern city of al-Hazm on Monday, killing seven people, including one child.
Jim Reid, of Deutsche Bank, said all of the latest developments have "left investors growing more concerned about further disruption and pricing a longer period of high energy prices."

title: Brent crude reaches $100 as war in Iran intensifies
